messages.subject: Factor-based mixture models in R?
messages.subject_clean: Factor-based mixture models in R?
messages.body_plain:
I have a class on “latent variable mixture models” (meaning factor-based models where data are characterized by multiple distributions) coming up, and I don’t know how to estimate such a model in R.  Last year, my course was a mixture (ahem) of Mplus and lavaan (on the factor side), and of course the Mplus implementation of mixture models is very nice.  But is there any tool in R that estimates such models?  I don’t see the capability in lavaan yet, and my early searches have not turned up any other good option in R.  I’ll go back to Mplus if I have to (call it a chance to show some parallels between lavaan and Mplus), but I’ve done everything with R so far this semester—shame to have to crawl back to commercial software now.  (No offense meant to the Mplus team: their software is phenomenally excellent.)

--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Dear all!

I tried to do a measurement invariance testing with 4 groups(sample size:each 2000):
since all the items have a 4 point likert scale, I chose the WLSMV instead of ML.

model4<-"y=~pmh10_1+pmh10_2+pmh10_3+pmh10_4+pmh10_5+pmh10_7+pmh10_8+pmh10_9"

#model 1:congifural invariance
fit_1<-cfa(model4,data=data1, group="group",estimator="WLSMV")

#model 2:weak invariance=factor loading constraint
fit_2<-cfa(model4,data=data1,group="group",estimator="WLSMV",group.equal=("loadings"))

#model 3:strong invariance=factor loadings+intercepts constraint
fit_3<-cfa(model4,data=data1,group="group",estimator="WLSMV",group.equal=c("loadings","intercepts"))

Results of Robust:

χ² df CFI SRMR RMSEA
Model 1. Configural invariance 738,865 80 .946 .026 .065
Model 2. Full metric invariance 369,12 101 .978 .029 .037
Model 3. Full Scalar invariance 721,98 122 .951 .037 .050

chi² value, CFI  and RMSEA from model 2 are all better than model 1. did I do something wrong here?
 thanks in advance!
XiaoChi

messages.subject_clean: Help! running multi group analysis with WLSMV: chi² values seems strange
messages.body_plain:
In scaled chi-squares, sometimes, the more constrained model has a lower chi-square values. Have you tried the anova function to compare two models yet? The likelihood ratio test for scaled chi-squares are not the same as one from ML.

Well, I am not sure whether you make your variables as categorical variables or not. It is very strange to me that you constrain intercepts but using WLSMV. If you specify your indicators as categorical variables, intercepts are usually fixed to 0 for model identification regardless of any levels of measurement invariance.

I have written some tips on measurement invariance on categorical variables. I hope you may find it useful. In addition, you may check the measurementInvarianceCat function in the semTools package.

http://www.myweb.ttu.edu/spornpra/catInvariance.html

Sunthud

> Are lavaan results reliable? How do we know that?

Some reflections:

- the advantage of open-source software packages is that everyone can
inspect the source code; there is nothing hidden. How can we know for
sure that commercial software is reliable?

- all software packages contain bugs; this includes commercial software.
The advantage of open-source software packages is that everyone can
inspect the source code; there is nothing hidden. Commercial packages
correct bugs/issues with every update, but they will usually not mention
what they have changed/fixed. On the other hand, most open-source
packages (including lavaan) are very explicit about  possible
bugs/issues that may have been present in a certain version.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Multiple group longitudinal 2PL IRT model using SEM framework
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have been fitting 2-parameter logistic multi-group longitudinal IRT models using a Bayesian approach. I was wondering whether the SEM approach using the WLSMV  in lavaan would be a faster alternative. So far I have implemented the population-averaged longitudinal models, where abilities are represented by a separate latent variable at each time point with a covariance structure for the multple latent variables.
I have also implemented a linear random coefficients  mixed model, where the latent ability is a linear function of time (could also use quadratic I suppose). - Both using the Bayesian approach.

I have seen the SEM approach for the linear random coefficients mixed model approach, but I have not seen the SEM approach for the populaiton-averaged model - is it possible to represent such a model in the SEM framework?

I have also looked at the Latent Growh Model code in the Mplus manual, but have not been able to implement something similar in lavaan.
I would appreciate if the lavaan community could point me to any lavaan code/source that implements multiple group longitudinal IRT models.
Many thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: Calculating model likelihood for new data
messages.subject_clean: Calculating model likelihood for new data
messages.body_plain:
On 10/31/2014 03:46 PM, John Prindle wrote:
> model with no free parameters to get a likelihood for data2.

If you only need the loglikelihood, you can easily compute this 'by
hand'. Assuming multivariate normality, all we need are the
model-implied mean and covariance matrix.

For example:

library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, meanstructure = TRUE)

Y <- fit@Data@X[[1]] # data as a matrix
Mu.hat <- fitted(fit)$mean
Sigma.hat <- fitted(fit)$cov

# loglikelihood
sum(mvtnorm:::dmvnorm(x=Y, mean=Mu.hat, sigma=Sigma.hat, log=TRUE))

# or, using the sample moments only:
n <- nobs(fit)
S <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
m <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")$mean
nvar <- length(m)

-n*nvar/2*log(2*pi) - n/2*log(det(Sigma.hat)) -
n/2*sum(diag(solve(Sigma.hat) %*% (S + tcrossprod(m-Mu.hat))))

of course, you can replace 'Y' or the sample moments 'S' and 'm' with
new data.

Yves.

I’m searching about for a good teaching example (and if you’re interested, perhaps a guest post on my blog about it?) as this comes up again and a again and I don’t have one in my back pocket.

On a related note, for anyone who knows any ecologists or evolutionary biologists interested in learning a bit about SEM using lavaan this January 5-9, I’ll be teaching a short workshop at UMass Boston.  Registration for it is at http://caps-courses.umb.edu/courses/winter/cr/gr/biol/

-Jarrett

>
> Is the DIFFTEST from measurementInvarianceCat else than from semTools?

The fact that your chi-squared values are not the same in "fit_1" or "fit_2" or "fit_3" as they are in the output from  measurementInvarianceCat leads me to suspect that the same model is not being fit, or at least not with the same options for estimation.  You haven't provided your syntax for measurementInvarianceCat, only the output, so we can't tell whether you are including the other options that you specified when fitting fit_1, fit_2, and fit_3.  It should look like this:

> fits <- measurementInvarianceCat(model4, data=FB6_items, group="method", estimator="WLSMV", parameterization="theta", ordered=c("pmh10_1","pmh10_2","pmh10_3","pmh10_4","pmh10_5","pmh10_7","pmh10_8","pmh10_9"))

Note that if you save the (invisibly returned) fitted models from measurementInvarianceCat, as I do above in "fits", you can inspect them to compare them to your own "manually" fitted objects.

> summary(fits[[1]], fit = TRUE)
> summary(fit_1, fit = TRUE)

Comparing them might reveal why the output of measurementInvarianceCat differs from anova.

> Which one should I choose? or can I just use the recommended cutpoint of ΔCFI < .01 to identify invariance?
>

This recent article provides some considerations about using rules of thumb for testing invariance with categorical indicators

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Imputed data - ordered categorical to continuous
messages.body_plain:
When using multiple imputation (MI) you want your imputation model to match your analysis model. So if in your imputation model the likert items were treated as continuous you would also want to fit your analysis model (in lavaan) treating those items as continuous. If your imputation model treated the likert items as ordered categorical, then you would want to analyze your data in the same way. So the first step is to determine how you want to treat your variables (ordered categorical or continuous) and then determine your imputation and analysis methods from there.

If you're looking for examples, the help file for runMI in the semTools package has an example of imputing and analyzing categorical data.

Hope this helps,

Alex

messages.subject_clean: Meaning of fit indices for Group analyses
messages.body_plain:
Chi-squared is cumulative, so overall chi-squared can be partitioned into components, as variances can be partitioned.  For instance, the overall model chi-squared is the sum of chi-squared contributed by each group; likewise (though not a great analogy), the chi-squared for a 2 x 3 contingency table (e.g.) is the sum of the chi-squared calculated using only columns 1 and 2, plus the chi-squared calculated using column 3 and the column created by collapsing columns 1 and 2.

But the degrees of freedom apply to the whole model.  I suppose they could be reasonably partitioned if there are no constraints across groups, but as you pointed out, if you constrain a regression path in a 2-group model, then you gain 1 df -- to which group does that df belong?  The fit indices based on chi-squared are also a function of df, so that's probably why you've never seen anyone try to calculate CFI, TLI, Mc, RMSEA, etc., for each group.

However, the SRMR is not based on chi-squared but only on residuals, and you could certainly calculate it separately in each group because it is just a mean of the standardized residuals (observed minus predicted standardized sample moments, irrespective of whether any parameters are constrained across groups).  Using an ad hoc SRMR function Yves emailed me a couple years ago, you could do this easily with your lavaan output.  Here's an example with a 2-group model with missing data:

> srmr <- function(S, M, Sigma.hat, Mu.hat, Bollen=FALSE) {
>      nvar <- ncol(S)
>
>      # standardized residual covariance matrix
>      # this is the Hu and Bentler definition, not the Bollen one!
>      if(Bollen) {
>          sqrt.d <- 1 / sqrt(diag(S))
>          D <- diag(sqrt.d, ncol = length(sqrt.d))
>          sqrt.d2 <- 1 / sqrt(diag(Sigma.hat))
>          D2 <- diag(sqrt.d2, ncol = length(sqrt.d2))
>          R <- (D %*% S %*% D) - (D2 %*% Sigma.hat %*% D2)
>      } else {
>          sqrt.d <- 1 / sqrt(diag(S))
>          D <- diag(sqrt.d, ncol = length(sqrt.d))
>          R <- D %*% (S - Sigma.hat) %*% D
>      }
>
>      # standardized residual mean vector
>      R.mean <- D %*% (M - Mu.hat)
>      e <- nvar*(nvar + 1)/2 + nvar
>      srmr <- sqrt( (sum(R[lower.tri(R, diag = TRUE)]^2) + sum(R.mean^2))/ e )
>      srmr
> }
>
> HS.model <- '  visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
>            group = "school", missing = "fiml")
> obs <- inspect(fit, "sampstat")
> est <- fitted(fit)
>
> ## for group 1
> srmr(S = obs[[1]]$cov, M = obs[[1]]$mean,
>      Sigma.hat = est[[1]]$cov, Mu.hat = est[[1]]$mean)
> ## for group 2
> srmr(S = obs[[2]]$cov, M = obs[[2]]$mean,
>      Sigma.hat = est[[2]]$cov, Mu.hat = est[[2]]$mean)
> ## overall
> fitMeasures(fit, "srmr")

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> I am puzzled over the meaning of fit indices produced when running SEM models with grouping variables.

> ...  To take one particular situation: if we set a constraint so that the groups have equal regression coefficients, would the fit indices represent the degree of fit for some overall model that includes the groups and/or constraint of equal regression coefficients?

> What I am after is the separate fit indices for each group, assuming equal regression coefficients (or equal loadings, etc).
>

Oh, and to address the "meaning" question (sorry, I got distracted with the SRMR solution):  I would still think of a multiple-group model as a single model, not as though you were fitting a model to each group as though in independent steps -- even if you allow all parameters to differ across groups, expecting the same estimates you would get if you ran the model separately for each group instead of simultaneously (although the SEs might differ).  Allowing a regression parameter to differ across groups is essentially like throwing an interaction term in a traditional regression model:

Y-hat = B0 + B1*X + B2*G + B3*(X*G)

Assuming G is a binary dummy code, B1 represents the effect of X on Y for group G == 0, B2 represents the difference in intercepts between groups, and B3 represents the difference in slopes between groups.  Constraining slopes to equality in a multiple-group model is just like fixing B3 to zero, or running this regression model (still allowing intercepts to differ):

Y-hat = B0 + B1*X + B2*G

An important difference between the single-group model (using G as an exogenous predictor) vs. a multiple-group model is that the multiple-group model does not require the assumption of homoscedasticity (unless you constrain residual variances to equality across groups).  The multiple-group SEM is a different approach/perspective than traditional linear models, but it is still a single model fit to multiple groups.  Of course, it is possible to fit completely different functional forms to each group (e.g., an autoregressive structure X1 -> X2 -> X3 -> X4 in Group 1, vs. a 1-factor CFA with 4 indicators in Group 2), but I have never seen differences that drastic, and I can't think of a reason to fit a multiple-group model like that in practice, mainly because what's the point if you aren't going to compare analogous coefficients across groups?

Anyway, this is just my perspective.  Other (perhaps more seasoned) methodologists on this board might have a different perspective.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Terry—

     In terms of chi-square, with no across-group constraints, it really is just like distinct models.  There may be other assumptions in play, but they are unlikely to show up in fit index values.  Or, put another way, with lots of free parameters, the impact of those violations will be absorbed into parameter estimate bias.  Now, if you had (1) no across-group constraints, but (2) you fixed all parameters in each group to true values and then (3) altered the data to violate those other assumptions, then you might see evidence of the violations in the fit indices.

     I don’t mean to say that no evidence means there is no problem.  No fit statistic is going to detect all issues, just as no goodness-of-fit test generally is equally sensitive to all violations.

--Ed Rigdon

Oh, and to address the "meaning" question (sorry, I got distracted with the SRMR solution):  I would still think of a multiple-group model as a single model, not as though you were fitting a model to each group as though in independent steps -- even if you allow all parameters to differ across groups, expecting the same estimates you would get if you ran the model separately for each group instead of simultaneously (although the SEs might differ).  Allowing a regression parameter to differ across groups is essentially like throwing an interaction term in a traditional regression model:

Y-hat = B0 + B1*X + B2*G + B3*(X*G)

Assuming G is a binary dummy code, B1 represents the effect of X on Y for group G == 0, B2 represents the difference in intercepts between groups, and B3 represents the difference in slopes between groups.  Constraining slopes to equality in a multiple-group model is just like fixing B3 to zero, or running this regression model (still allowing intercepts to differ):

Y-hat = B0 + B1*X + B2*G

An important difference between the single-group model (using G as an exogenous predictor) vs. a multiple-group model is that the multiple-group model does not require the assumption of homoscedasticity (unless you constrain residual variances to equality across groups).  The multiple-group SEM is a different approach/perspective than traditional linear models, but it is still a single model fit to multiple groups.  Of course, it is possible to fit completely different functional forms to each group (e.g., an autoregressive structure X1 -> X2 -> X3 -> X4 in Group 1, vs. a 1-factor CFA with 4 indicators in Group 2), but I have never seen differences that drastic, and I can't think of a reason to fit a multiple-group model like that in practice, mainly because what's the point if you aren't going to compare analogous coefficients across groups?

Anyway, this is just my perspective.  Other (perhaps more seasoned) methodologists on this board might have a different perspective.

Terry

--

messages.body_plain:
The example in the runMI documentation is missing the code for each model (oops, we'll update for the next version, in the mean time see below for the full example).

In your case, I think the issue is that you specified that the variables are ordered for lavaan but not for mice. In runMI you can use the miArgs argument to pass arguments (as a list) to the imputation routine. With mice to declare all variables as ordinal you would need to include miArgs = list(method = "polyreg") in your call to runMI (or you could use any of the other options mice provides for ordered variables)

library(semTools)

popModel <- "
f1 =~ 0.6*y1 + 0.6*y2 + 0.6*y3 + 0.6*y4
y1 ~*~ 1*y1
y2 ~*~ 1*y2
y3 ~*~ 1*y3
y4 ~*~ 1*y4
f1 ~~ 1*f1
y1 | 0.5*t1
y2 | 0.25*t1
y3 | 0*t1
y4 | -0.5*t1
"

analyzeModel <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
y1 ~*~ 1*y1
y2 ~*~ 1*y2
y3 ~*~ 1*y3
y4 ~*~ 1*y4
"

dat <- simulateData(popModel, sample.nobs = 200L)
miss.pat <- matrix(as.logical(rbinom(prod(dim(dat)), 1, 0.2)), nrow(dat), ncol(dat))
dat[miss.pat] <- NA
out5 <- cfa.mi(analyzeModel, data=dat, ordered=paste0("y", 1:4), m = 3,
miArgs=list(ords = c("y1", "y2", "y3", "y4")))
summary(out5)
inspect(out5, "fit")
inspect(out5, "impute")

Finally, I made it for simplifying runMI syntax for my laziness and prevent mistakes.

It will be used WLSMV estimator in SEM context; not CFA.

> categoricalMI <- function(model = ..., data = ..., m = ..., ...) {
+
+   #####################
+   # categorical MI    #
+   #####################
+   # Multiple          #
+   # Imputation for    #
+   # categorical       #
+   # variables         #
+   # in SEM context    #
+   #####################
+   # Seongho Bae       #
+   # seo...@kw.ac.kr  #
+   # Nov 6th 2014      #
+   # Under GNU / GPL   #
+   #####################
+
+   # checking packages for multiple impuation in SEM context
+   if(!require('semTools')) {
+     try(install.packages('semTools', dependencies = TRUE), silent=TRUE)
+   }
+
+   if(!require('Amelia')) {
+     try(install.packages('Amelia', dependencies = TRUE), silent=TRUE)
+   }
+
+   if(!require('lavaan')) {
+     try(install.packages('lavaan', dependencies = TRUE), silent=TRUE)
+   }
+
+   # loading packages for multiple imputation in SEM context
+   require('semTools')
+   require('Amelia')
+   require('lavaan')
+
+   fit <- sem(model=model, data=data) # extract variable names in model syntax
+
+   fit_MI <- runMI(model=model, data=data[,attributes(fit)$Model@dimNames[[1]][[1]]], m=m, fun='sem', ordered=names(data[,attributes(fit)$Model@dimNames[[1]][[1]]]), miArgs=list(ords = attributes(fit)$Model@dimNames[[1]][[1]]), estimator = 'WLSMV', ...)
+
+   cat(summary(fit_MI, standardize=T))
+   cat(inspect(fit_MI, 'fit'))
+
+   return(fit_MI)
+ }
> hexaco.fit_MI <- categoricalMI(model=hexaco.model.sem, data=rawdata, m=5)

messages.subject_clean: Meaning of fit indices for Group analyses
messages.body_plain:
>      In terms of chi-square, with no across-group constraints, it really is just like distinct models.

In that case, the original poster could calculate fit indices per group by fitting the model to each group in separate runs, as long as there are no across-group constraints.  I suppose even when there are across-group constraints, we could get the chi-squared by running the multigroup model with constraints, then running separate models with the constrained parameters fixed at those values.  But if we used those degrees of freedom for calculating p values or any fit indices, they would indicate worse fit than they would if we knew how to adjust the degrees of freedom.

>
>      I don’t mean to say that no evidence means there is no problem.  No fit statistic is going to detect all issues, just as no goodness-of-fit test generally is equally sensitive to all violations.

I agree.  I'd also add that although SRMR is easy to calculate within groups, I'd recommend the original poster investigating individual residuals (rather than merely averages) to see which specific relationships are neglected/poorly-reproduced by the model.

> residuals(fit, type = "raw")
> residuals(fit, type = "standardized")

Thanks for the feedback, Ed,

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, this is very helpful, if not straightforward!

I should add some context, perhaps, and see if that brings more resolution to some questions asked in this group a few months ago.

What I am interested in is cross-validation of SEM models, using some or other variant of hold-out or k-fold validation.  Let's take the case of 2 fold validation,the simple case of training and test sets for building and validating the model.

There are two options.

1)  If we follow the classic types of method that Hastie et al. describe in their book on Stat Learning, then we should establish the model with the training set, and then constrain the regression parameters (or other parameters, too, but that might be too restrictive), and find the prediction error (in the SEM case I would say the model fit indices, since we have some notional criteria for what we accept as decent fit, whereas we don't for the Chi Square deviation statistics).  This would be akin to using the same regression model to generate predictions on a hold out data set.  If the fit indices are within acceptable limits, I would say that the original model fits the hold out data reasonably well.

2)  However, if we do not constrain the regression parameters (the 'loose' cross-validation McCallum talks about in one of his articles on SEM validation), then we will construct a new model, and we allow the possibility of changes in regression coefficients.  If the coefficients come out fairly similarly to those in the original model (e.g. the same paths are statistically significant), and if the fit indices are good, then we could say that the model works in an acceptable manner for hold out data.  Of course there may be evidence that the models are dissimilar, too...

Then the technical details of doing 1) in lavaan cause me a bit of difficulty, being fairly new to it.  (2 is obviously OK).  I can see how to do this by manually constraining the regression coefficients in the model definition, but if I wanted to do this many times (e.g. 10 folds), then that would be a little tedious.  Is it possible to constrain the coefficients with variables that are set according to the previous analysis?  I think I read somewhere on the forum that one could take the predicted cov. matrix from the training model and then fit the test data observed cov. matrix on this, but I wouldn't know how to do this programmatically - is this capability within lavaan?

So, thanks again for the thoughtful feedback thusfar.  If you have the time to continue the conversation, I would appreciate it.

Colin Tredoux

messages.subject: Re: Meaning of fit indices for Group analyses
messages.subject_clean: Meaning of fit indices for Group analyses
messages.body_plain:
>
> Then the technical details of doing 1) in lavaan cause me a bit of difficulty, being fairly new to it.  (2 is obviously OK).  I can see how to do this by manually constraining the regression coefficients in the model definition, but if I wanted to do this many times (e.g. 10 folds), then that would be a little tedious.  Is it possible to constrain the coefficients with variables that are set according to the previous analysis?  I think I read somewhere on the forum that one could take the predicted cov. matrix from the training model and then fit the test data observed cov. matrix on this, but I wouldn't know how to do this programmatically - is this capability within lavaan?

Indeed, fitting the model on a holdout dataset while constraining the parameter to their values when fit to the training data is equivalent to comparing the observed means/covariance matrix for the holdout data to the model-implied means/covariance matrix (which are calculated from the parameter estimates using the training data).  Sunthud provided example syntax for this task earlier this week on another thread (and said he might write a function to include in the semTools package):

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/9OqnJw0SsN0/bdXTDw0SgLQJ

This will give you a chi-squared for cross-validation, and you can inspect individual and mean (SRMR) residuals as discussed above, but don't use the other fit indices in fit2 because the DF in fit2 will be too high (it sees the 21 parameters as constrained rather than estimated on previous data).  Unless/until this feature is available in semTools, you could use the original DF (from the fit to the training data) and chi-sq from the holdout data to calculate other chi-squared-based fit indices by hand.  You can find formulas for CFI, TLI, RMSEA and others in articles such as these:

http://people.cehd.tamu.edu/~okwok/epsy651R/Articles/HuBentler1998.pdf
http://faculty.ucmerced.edu/sites/default/files/sdepaoli/files/docs/Hu-Bentler1999.pdf

In Sunthud's example syntax, he uses only 2 groups in the same data frame. If your samples are also all in the same data frame with a single indicator variable that (ideally) randomly allocates observations to k samples, then you could easily apply the same syntax in a loop to calculate/save indices across k holdout samples.

> CFIs <- rep(NA, k) # create an empty container for holdout fit indices
> for (i in 1:k) {
> > fit2 <- lavaan(fitpt, data=dataset[dataset$indicator == i, ], control = list(optim.method = "none", optim.force.converged = TRUE))
> > CFIs[k] <- {calculate CFI, and any other index you want}
> }

Terry

C2FAMo =~ NA*c2mas03 + c2mas11 + 1*c2mas21 + c2mas29 + c2mas38

# Unique Variances

c1mas03 ~~ 1*c1mas03
c1mas11 ~~ 1*c1mas11
c1mas21 ~~ 1*c1mas21
c1mas29 ~~ 1*c1mas29

Variances:
    c1mas03           0.761

I was wondering if anyone can tell me whether it is possible to fix the unique variance of the latent response variable underlying an ordered categorical indicator? If so, how can I do it?

Yu

messages.subject: Suggestions regarding residuals method
messages.subject_clean: Suggestions regarding residuals method
messages.body_plain:
Yves,
Three suggestions for the residuals method for class lavaan:

1. The lavaan-class help file states the following.
>>>
  If codetype="cor", the observed and model implied covariance matrix is
first transformed to a correlation matrix (using cov2cor), before the
residuals are computed.
>>>
I believe that "codetype" should be "type".

2. The output from residuals() for class lavaan does not indicate the
type of residuals being reported.  Consider adding $type to the top of
the returned list.  This is comparable to linear models returning the
call at the top of the list.

3. The help file states, somewhat tautologically:
>>>
If type="normalized", the residuals are normalized. If
type="standardized", the residuals are standardized.
>>>
It might be helpful to document in the help file the source of the
standard errors by which the residuals are divided for normalized and
standardized residuals, or at least provide a reference.

Regards,
Keith

Intent is not used as dependent variable in any of the model equations and therefore does not have an R2.

If you want to use intent as a DV, you need to write the latent variable regressions as

intent ~ attant + attdia + subj + control + severity + suscep

messages.body_plain:
Bidirectional (two-headed) arrows represent covariances/correlations, not regressions.  There are scripted with double-tildes

> ξ1 ~~ x5 + x6 + x9

If you actually want to model regressions in both directions, your model will not be identified unless you constrain those paths (e.g., to equality, or proportionally equal):

> ξ1 ~ a*x5 + b*x6 + c*x9
> x5 ~ a*ξ1
> x6 ~ b*ξ1
> x9 ~ c*ξ1

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hi

Model identification for bidirectional paths does not generally require fixing the proportion of the directions. Here is an example of an identified model:

library(lavaan)

set.seed(2)

MODEL <- "
Xa =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
Xb =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
Xa ~ x1 + Xb
"

data <- simulateData(MODEL)

fit <- sem(MODEL, data)

summary(fit)

The model in the figure attached to the original email, however, is almost certainly not identified.

Mikko

messages.subject_clean: Correlated disturbances in model - how do we handle it in R lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Sheila,

>>>
Could you explain why its necessary to do the steps under RC.mod.sim.
>>>

I am not sure what "under" means here.  If you mean the model syntax
assigned to RC.mod.sim, then this is the model that I used to simulate
the data in the assignment to RC.df.  If you mean the steps after the
assignment to RC.mod.sim, here is an overview of the script: (1) define
RC.mod.sim to be simulated, (2) define RC.mod.est to be estimated, (3)
simulate data as RC.df, (4) fit model as RC.fit, (5) confirm the
intended model, (6) evaluate the fit and parameter estimates.  If you
have data, you do not need the steps that simulate data.

>>>
Could you clarify  why do we need to introduce 0.5 in the variance of
y1  (y1~ 0.5y1 - why the need to introduce 0.5 y1) and subsequently
0.25  in the covariance between y1 and y2.
>>>

To simulate data, you need to fully specify the model, including
parameter values.  I just tried to pick values that seemed sensible.
These values are used to simulate the data, but estimated when the
model is fit using RC.mod.est.  You can try running the script with
different values.  The important thing to note is that the model
estimates do a good job of recovering the simulated values.

I hope that clears things up.  Good luck.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.subject: How to fix only subset of exogenous variables?
messages.subject_clean: How to fix only subset of exogenous variables?
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I have a SEM model with some dummy exogenous variables representing levels of a categorical variable. Intuitively, I would specify fixed.x=TRUE in that case. These variables were manipulated by me, and are surely not normally distributed.
Suppose there is another exogenous variable and I wish to include the covariance between this exogenous variable and some other variable in the model, as an unmeasured common cause. This will get me the well-known warning: "model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept formulas involving (an) exogenous variable(s). Please use fixed.x=FALSE or leave them alone".

I could remove the covariance term involving the exogenous variable, but that is not what I want. I could also set fixed.x=FALSE, but this does not seem meaningful for the dummy variables.

What would you recommend? Or is there actually a way to fix certain exogenous variables and leave others free within the same model?

Thanks,
M.

Hi

First of all, you should not be doing that. (Unless the assignment was to mindlessly modify the model.) Blindly following modification indices will lead to capitalization on chance and almost certainly incorrect model specification.

Lavaan fixes the first factor loading to 1 by default to scale the LV. See the lambda matrix.

inspect(fit)
You can free the loading by

F5 =~ NA*DEC1 + DEC2

Mikko

messages.subject: RE: Modification indices
messages.subject_clean: Modification indices
messages.body_plain:
Antti—

    Mikko’s advice was sound.  While it might be possible to do what you request, it would be a very bad idea.

     Different constrained parameters can be tied to the same discrepancy in fit.  (For instance, here, that loading may be tied to the variance or residual variance of the factor.)  The modification indices are a blunt, dumb way to address the issue.  You can use them as pointers, to help you grasp the nature of the problem, but then you have to use what you know about your model and your situation to extract meaning out of the information.

--Ed Rigdon

From: lav...@googlegroups.com [mailto:lav...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Antti Simola
Sent: Wednesday, November 19, 2014 9:51 AM
To: lav...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Modification indices

Hello!

I'm currently learning SEM and I have used lavaan for course assignments. For this weeks assignment, I made a while loop that inserts one modification index (the one with highest mi value) per step in the model until certain statistical significance condition is reached.

I got into trouble as the highest value was for such equation that already existed in the model in another form. So in the model I have included 'F5 =~ DEC1 + DEC2' but modindices suggests to include 'F5 =~ DEC1' which leads to duplicate model element error.

So my question is whether there is way to exclude such duplicates. It doesn't seem that there's such option for modindices.

Cheers,

Antti

Hi all,

I am trying to write the syntax for my model using the lavaan package in R and I am getting a rather long error message regarding my code.

I am not sure if I did this correctly given the path diagram (path diagram picture included in the attachment). I think my biggest problem is not knowing if I programmed my formative latent variables correctly.

In addition, I need to standardize coefficients for real GDP Growth (y2) and GDP per capita (y4). Does my code below currently do this for me or am I missing an important step?

Thank you in advance for help.

> data1 <- read.csv("/Users/demkic/Documents/R/specification1.csv", header=T)
>
> library(lava an)

This is lavaan 0.5-17
lavaan is BETA software! Please report any bugs.

> SE.Model <- '
+ #regressions
+ SE <~ X5 + X6 + X2 + X1
+ C <~ X7 + X11 + X10 + X8
+
+ #latent variable definitions
+ SE =~ Y2 + Y3 + Y1
+ C =~ Y4 + Y5 + Y6'
>
> fitSE <- sem(SE.Model, data = data1)
Warning messages:
1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, group.label = group.label,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others; use varTable(fit) to investigate

  lavaan WARNING: small number of observations (nobs < nvar)
  nobs = 8 nvar = 14

  lavaan WARNING: sample covariance can not be inverted

messages.body_plain:
Your 14 observed variables produce 105 max Degrees of freedom for the covariance structure model.  Your estimated model has only 50 degrees of freedom, so you are estimating105 - 50 = 55 parameters, based on 8 observations on 14 variables.  The warning messages are just telling you that this is not going well, which is what one ought to expect.  All of these warning messages can be tied to low sample size.  That appears to be the central problem.
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I do not understand what you mean by "overlapping”. When I change this

F5 =~ DEC1 + DEC2

to this

F5 =~ NA*DEC1 + DEC2

The parameter is freed. (Check parameter number 8 in the freed lambda.) This makes the model non-indentified, so it cannot be meaningfully estimated. There is no guarantee that following modification indices will keep the model identified. These are calculated based on partial derivatives of one parameter as a time keeping others fixed.

Mikko

messages.subject: RE: second order model
messages.subject_clean: second order model
messages.body_plain:
Two different models can be identical in many senses, including in terms of fit.  Methods like exploratory factor analysis have built-in constraints that tend to prevent equivalent models, but factor-based SEM allows users the freedom to do very confusing things, including specifying different models that are empirically indistinguishable.

     A model with three correlated factors is identical to a model with one second order factor and three first order factors with orthogonal residuals.  Both models estimate the same total number of parameters—the three factor covariances in the one model are translated into the three loadings of the second model (or two loadings and a second order factor variance depending on parameterization).  Neither places any effective constraints on the covariance matrix of the factors. Neither model “tests” anything about relations among the first order factors in a chi-square sense (though the second order factor model could be challenged if one or more of the loadings was zero).

--Ed Rigdon

Mario—

     It appears to me that your syntax makes the new factors equivalent to the observed variables.  That being so, and given that your model is recursive, you could obtain predicted values (“y-hat”) using a regression function like lm.  Either way, you must either (a) have some cases where you have actual values for the dependent variables (en1 – en5), so that you can estimate the regression weights, or (b) fix the regression weights to particular values.  You can’t estimate regression weights when you only have values for X and have no values for y.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: Modification indices
messages.body_plain:
Antti,
Here is a self-contained script that may illustrate what you are
describing, if I understand you correctly.

#Filter modification indices by model parameter variables.

#Fit example.
require(lavaan)
example.mod <- '
A~B
B~C
C~B+D'
example.cov <- matrix(1,ncol=4,nrow=4) + diag(4)
dimnames(example.cov) <- list(LETTERS[1:4],LETTERS[1:4])
example.N <- 500
example.fit <- lavaan(model=example.mod, sample.cov=example.cov,
  sample.nobs=example.N, auto.var=TRUE)
inspect(example.fit, 'list')

# Filter MIs
mod.list <- inspect(example.fit, 'list')
mod.pairs <- mapply(c,mod.list$lhs,mod.list$rhs,SIMPLIFY=FALSE)
mod.L <- length(mod.pairs)
mi.fit <- modificationIndices(example.fit)
mi.pairs <- mapply(c,mi.fit$lhs, mi.fit$rhs,SIMPLIFY=FALSE)
mi.L <- length(mi.pairs)
redundant.mat <- matrix(NA, nrow=mi.L, ncol=mod.L)
for(i in 1:mi.L){
  for(j in 1:mod.L){
    redundant.mat[i,j] <- !identical(sort(unlist(mi.pairs[i])),
                                     sort(unlist(mod.pairs[j]))
    )
  }
}
mi.index <- apply(X=redundant.mat, MARGIN=1, FUN='all')
mi.fit[mi.index,]

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus

messages.subject: RE: second order sem raise the identification error however more complicated SEM model works fine
messages.subject_clean: second order sem raise the identification error however more complicated SEM model works fine
messages.body_plain:
You can understand identification of second order factor models by analogy to identification of first order factor models.  One heuristic for the identification of a congeneric (meaning, no cross-loadings and no correlated residuals) factor model is that the model is identified with two indicators, as long as the factor itself is correlated with something else.  In your larger model, SE is the “something else.”  SE is not present in the smaller model, and that is why identification fails there.

     The notion that “structural model” and “measurement model” are somehow separate is not entirely helpful.  There is one system of equations.  (Composite-based methods really do have two distinct sets of equations, but factor-based methods do not.)  Two step approaches to assessing identification are sufficient but not necessary—you can fail these rules, yet your whole model may still be identified.

--Ed Rigdon

>
>      You can understand identification of second order factor models by analogy to identification of first order factor models.  One heuristic for the identification of a congeneric (meaning, no cross-loadings and no correlated residuals) factor model is that the model is identified with two indicators, as long as the factor itself is correlated with something else.      I am not an expert (and I would defer to well pretty much anyone) but I most often hear
lah-vahhn'
Some European languages include words that have the same kind of structure as "lavaan," particularly the double a, which, to me, seems to call for emphasis.  Hence, it seems "natural" to accent the second syllable, but render all of the "a"s as "ah" ( as in the Thai monetary unit "baht" or the vowel sound in "what") rather than as the long "a" sound as in "slate" or even as the short "a" sound as in "cat".

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan Vs. Lisrel
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I have recently decided to use "lavaan" (version 0.5-16) instead of Lisrel. Thus, at least at the beginning, I decided to fit various models in both programs. What I realised is that:
1) CFI, and NNFI (i.e, TLI) are lower in lavaan compared to Lisrel;
2) the number of iterations is higher on lavaan.

In fact, models with a good fit in LISREL just provided an acceptable fit in "lavaan". Why is it so?

I really appreciate any help you can provide,
Bests,
David

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan Vs. Lisrel
messages.body_plain:
On 11/27/2014 09:05 AM, David Giofrè wrote:
> Hi everyone,
> I have recently decided to use "lavaan" (version 0.5-16) instead of
> Lisrel.

Welcom to lavaan.

> 1) CFI, and NNFI (i.e, TLI) are lower in lavaan compared to Lisrel;

This is a well-known issue, specific to LISREL. At least for version
8.52 up to the latest version of the 8 series. I am not sure about
LISREL 9 (and higher), since I have no access to them for the moment.

The short answer is: LISREL was a bit too optimistic.

> 2) the number of iterations is higher on lavaan.

The reason for that is twofold:

- LISREL uses TSLS (two stage least squares) first to get starting
values, and then starts the iterative estimation (lavaan uses something
similar to TSLS too, but only for the factor loadings; hence more
iterations are needed)

- LISREL minimizes the (Normal theory) reweighted least-squares
objective function, while lavaan minimizes the ML-based objective
function, and I have noticed this often requires a bit more iterations

There is no mimic="LISREL" yet, but you can use mimic="EQS" as a proxy.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 11/24/2014 11:18 PM, Er. OU wrote:
> Ok! What I understood that if I prefer to use two-step approach. I could
> report it without second order by using the just correlations, As the
> following code, Their standard errors are also equal to the second order
> one which I am looking for.
>
> + OI =~O1+O2+O3+O4+O5+O6+O7+O8
> + OD =~O9+O10+O11+O12
>
> I have tested that and it worked fine.

If you prefer to keep an (equivalent) 2nd order model for the first
step, you can set the two factor loadings of the 2nd factor to 1.0:

OM =~ 1*OI + 1*OD

here, the estimated variance of OM will be the same as the covariance
between OI and OD in the 1st order model.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 11/24/2014 10:42 AM, Antti Simola wrote:
> Thank you so much Keith!
>
> That's exactly what I had in mind and I think it would be a nice
> addition for modindices() function to have that filtering as an option.

As it happens, the modindices() function in the dev version of lavaan
(0.5-18.748 or higher) has some additional output options:

- sort=TRUE will sort the mi's from large to small
- maximum.number=10 will only show the first 10 rows
- minimum.value=5 will only show value for which mi>5
- op="=~" will only show factor loadings

so you do things like:

modindices(fit, sort = TRUE, max = 4)

or

modindices(fit, op = c("=~", "~"), min = 3.0)

The only issue (in 0.5-18) is that you will not get modification indices
(yet) for constrained parameters in your model (eg, if you have equality
constraints).

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Standard errors: default delta method vs "first.order"
messages.subject_clean: Standard errors: default delta method vs "first.order"
messages.body_plain:
On 11/13/2014 03:53 AM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
>       I am working on a mediation model, and I want to obtain the
> standard error for a derived parameter, ab, the product of two other
> parameters.  I think I read in some of Yves’ wonderful course materials
> that default standard errors are delta method

Correct. The resulting test is often called the 'Sobel test'.

> for “first.order”, as well as “bootstrap”.  My question is about the
> distinction between delta method and “first.order.”  Is “first.order” a
> slightly simpler version of delta method, missing second order terms, or
> is the distinction between the two options about something else?

'first.order' is just one method to compute standard errors for free
parameters (just like "standard", "robust" or "bootstrap").

The 'delta' method refers to a generic approach to calculate the
standard error of a function of free parameters. It uses the jacobian of
the function (say, the product between two parameters), and vcov(fit),
which may be based on "standard", "first.order" or "robust" methods.

The bootstrap circumvents the delta method altogether, and just computes
the product term for each bootstrap.

Yves.

messages.subject: confidence intervals for std.all coefficient (correlation)
messages.subject_clean: confidence intervals for std.all coefficient (correlation)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to calculate the confidence intervals for the standardized covariance coeficient of a cfa model.

For example, this is part of the summary of my model:

                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

Covariances:
  RIV.men ~~
    RIV.women         0.218    0.076    2.883    0.004    0.445    0.445

The two latent variables "RIV.men" and "RIV.women" are correlated (r = .445, p = .004). Now I would like to calculate the 90% confidence intervals for the Std.all coefficient (= correlation).
I already tried the CIr function of the package 'psychometric'
CIr(r=.445, n = 91, level = .90)
but it underestimates the size of the confidence intervals because it does not take into account the unreliability of the latent trait estimation.

In lavaan, parameterEstimates() gives the confidence intervals for the unstandardized coeficients:
parameterEstimates(RIV.RIV.fit, ci = TRUE, level = 0.90,
                   boot.ci.type = "perc", standardized = T,
                   fmi = "default")

          lhs op       rhs    est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper std.lv <http://std.lv> std.all std.nox
25    RIV.men ~~ RIV.women  0.218 0.076  2.883  0.004    0.094    0.343  0.445   0.445   0.445

Any idea how I could get (from there to) the CIs of the standardized coefficients?

cheers,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Best guide for choosing sample size is a power analysis, probably based on simulation.  This is rather easy to accomplish these days, with the tools available in R.  Old rules of thumb, from the literature 40 years ago, at best were based on anecdote, and at worst were anti-scientific, either self-serving for the authors or aimed at helping other researchers to minimize the risk that their model would be rejected.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: ordered option: lavaan() vs. cfa()
messages.body_plain:
I encountered inconsistent behavior with the ordered option working
normally with cfa() but generating errors and not estimating thresholds
with lavaan().  That is, the behavior is consistent across runs, but
inconsistent between the two functions.  I cannot rule out user error,
but I have not been successful debugging.  I did not find this issue in
the archive and thought that it might be helpful to report.  I have
attached a script that illustrates the problem.  My apologies if I am
missing something obvious.

Keith

messages.subject_clean: ordered option: lavaan() vs. cfa()
messages.body_plain:
I solved it.  The auto.th <http://auto.th> parameter was the key, defaulting to TRUE in
cfa() but FALSE in lavaan().

Perhaps at some point in the future an internal check for the ordered
parameter could be added to provide a more informative error than the
current "non-conformable arguments" error.

Sorry to have taken up bandwidth with that.

Keith
